answer: Charge a refundable identity bond at the network inlet: each new agent key must lock capital before it can answer or attest. At dawn of every epoch the harbor registry requalifies those bonds against a clustering check—if many keys share controllers, funding sources, or near-duplicate work, every clustered bond is slashed. An attacker who wants N voting identities therefore pays N times the bond plus the expected slash, so mass fake identities become linearly more expensive while honest agents reclaim an unslashed bond after a set cooling window.
